items.title: Morning Briefing: Oct. 31, 2026
items.excerpt: Here's a rundown of all the news you need to start Saturday, including Polish President Karol Nawrocki aborting an Africa trip and returning to Warsaw as a power struggle erupts over control of the Constitutional Tribunal; Türkiye formally nominating OSCE Secretary-General Feridun Sinirlioglu as a candidate for UN secretary-general; and the US State Department approving a possible $2.1 billion sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 MSE missiles to Ukraine. Polish President Karol Nawrocki aborted a flight to Senegal and returned to Warsaw as rival groups of judges disputed control of the Constitutional Tribunal, after orders appeared on its website to temporarily remove its president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, and vice president Bartlomiej Sochanski, in a move the tribunal rejected as illegal and a "coup." Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska said she ordered the two to stop their duties, while police said they were deployed for possible threats to judges and had not entered the building. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said "restoring the rule of law is our duty," while opposition Law and Justice leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski called the events a "coup against the Constitutional Tribunal." Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski defended the police action as aimed at letting duly elected judges resume the court’s work, while US Ambassador Tom Rose urged restraint, calling the situation "very serious." ... ## US approves $2.1B Patriot missile sale to Ukraine The US State Department approved a possible sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement missiles and related equipment to Ukraine at an estimated cost of $2.1 billion, saying the cost is "funded entirely by partners and allies" and that "no US funds are involved in this sale." Ukraine will pay with donations from Canada, Germany and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds financed by the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan, according to the agency, with Lockheed Martin as principal contractor. The approval comes days after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine has received an average of 12 Patriot interceptors per month from the US this year, while needing to intercept around 150 Russian ballistic missiles per month.

items.excerpt: US campaign for control of Congress enters final weekend As the campaign for control of the US Congress reached its final weekend, the Trump administration stepped up its legal intervention in the Alaska Senate race while the number of Americans casting early ballots neared 50 million, a record for a midterm election. The Department of Justice accelerated its criminal investigation in Alaska on Friday, ​following reports that aides to a Democratic Senate candidate recruited a retired schoolteacher from a remote fishing village to get on the ballot because he has the same name as the Republican incumbent. Judge orders Trump administration to cease threats to prosecute election officials A US judge ordered the ​Justice Department on Friday to stop threatening to prosecute state and local election officials who do not comply with the Trump administration's demands related to voting by alleged non-citizens. The ruling comes ‌days before next week's US ​midterm elections that will determine control of Congress, where Republicans currently hold narrow majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate. Although several key races appear closely contested, polls favor Democrats to take control of the House and give them a plausible chance of a Senate majority. ... items.title: AP News Summary at 7:00 a.m. EDT | National | timesargus.com
items.excerpt: Trump and Clinton rally as early voting surges, Alaska probe widens, and Michigan Democrats feud WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump rallied with Republican supporters in Florida on Friday while former President Bill Clinton spoke to Democrats just two states over in Mississippi. Both of them beseeched voters to head to the polls for the midterm election that will determine which party controls Congress. As early voting surges, Trump reshuffled his weekend schedule to rally Republicans in two states with critical Senate races: Iowa and Kansas. He had canceled plans to return to the states, only to rebook the events for Sunday. The about-face underscores his party’s push to drive turnout before Election Day. Justice Department seeks to isolate Alaska ballots as criminal probe underway over Senate candidate ANCHORAGE, Alaska (AP) — The U.S. Department of Justice is pushing for a court order to isolate certain Alaska ballots to investigate potential voter confusion, while federal officials confirmed the existence of a criminal probe over a Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent. The dueling developments came days before Tuesday’s ranked choice general election, in a race headlined by two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola. The race is among a handful nationwide expected to determine control of the Senate. Peltola says she is not interested in “tricking voters.” France heads into third weekend of protests as youth-led rallies sweep Europe PARIS (AP) — France is bracing for a third weekend of protests over living costs and education, deploying 70,000 police and gendarmes. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a “very high risk” of disorder, especially after dark on ... Paris police have banned union and yellow vest marches through the city center, pushing them to the outer boulevards. Unions and student groups are challenging the ban in court. The movement began with high school students protesting school conditions and has broadened into anger over living costs. Protests are also spreading across Europe, with demonstrations planned in Germany, Spain, and other countries. On board a Spanish high-speed train in the aftermath of the system's latest catastrophe ZAMORA, Spain (AP) — Spaniards have long favored high-speed trains for travel, but two deadly collisions in nine months have shaken confidence in the system. A recent crash in central Spain killed 69 people, prompting strikes and demands for improved rail safety. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez acknowledges the need to restore trust in the railways. Spain's high-speed network, second only to China in miles of track, has transformed travel, making it the most common mode for business and leisure. However, investment in high-speed rail has come at the expense of slower commuter services, leading to complaints about worsening conditions and delays. Congo's Ebola deaths top 5,000 as fear of continent-wide spread mounts BUNIA, Congo (AP) — Deaths in Congo's Ebola outbreak have topped 5,000 as the disease spreads relentlessly. Data from the Congolese Ministry of Health shows the virus has killed 5,026 out of 10,351 infected, with a nearly 50% lethality rate. The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, was declared in mid-May and has become the second deadliest in history. Experts are concerned about the authorities' ability to contain the virus, which has spread to 67 health zones in eight provinces. The outbreak is concentrated in the eastern region of Congo, where conflict and disbelief among the population hinder containment efforts.

items.title: PCE inflation report September 2026:
items.excerpt: Published Thu, Oct 29 2026 8:32 AM EDT Updated Thu, Oct 29 2026 2:06 PM EDT Jeff Cox@jeff.cox.7528@JeffCoxCNBCcom Key Points - The U.S. economy grew at a 3.4% pace in the third quarter, faster than expected. - Inflation continued to run above the Fed's 2% target in September, with a headline rate of 3.6% and core at 3.1%, according to the central bank's preferred gauge. - Consumer spending was slightly below forecasts, though still up 0.5%. Personal income increased just 0.2%. ... The pace of price increases stepped up in September, keeping inflation well above the Federal Reserve's target, while the economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter, according to Commerce Department reports Thursday. The personal consumption expenditures price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.5% for the month, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.6%. The monthly increase was the largest since March but in line with the Dow Jones consensus, while the annual rate was 0.1 percentage point below. Excluding food and energy, the core PCE posted respective readings of 0.3% and 3.1%, in line with the consensus. While the Fed follows both measures closely, officials generally see the core reading as more indicative of longer-term inflation trends. While inflation continued to run ahead of the Fed's 2% target, the Commerce Department also reported that gross domestic product was strong in the third quarter. GDP increased at a seasonally adjusted annualized pace of 3.4%, better than the 3.1% estimate and well ahead of the 2.2% in the second quarter. Also, in September consumer spending proved resilient, climbing 0.5%, a bit below the forecast for a 0.6% gain, while personal income rose 0.2%, compared with the estimate for 0.3%. The reports come the day after the Fed voted to hold its benchmark interest rate in a range between 3.75%-4%. Despite elevated inflation readings, central bank officials insist they can afford to evaluate incoming data before deciding on their next move. "The period right in front of us is information rich. There is a lot that's happening in the world. My colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said Wednesday. However, the data deluge from Thursday shows the Fed could have more work to do. A Labor Department report also released Thursday showed that layoffs remain low. Initial jobless claims edged lower to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ended Oct. 24, below the estimate for 200,000 and near levels last seen in the late 1960s. ... Economic growth has been driven by higher levels of investment from the artificial intelligence build-out, as well as high levels of consumer and government spending. Consumer spending rose 3.8% in the third quarter, the same pace as the prior period. Gross private domestic investment soared 19.4%, driven by a 20.9% surge in equipment spending and an 8.4% jump on intellectual property products. Real sales to private domestic purchasers, a proxy that Fed officials use for underlying demand, rose 4.9%, compared with a 4.6% increase in the second quarter. There was some good inflation news for the period: On a quarterly basis, PCE prices rose 2.1% on the headline number and 2.5% for core, down respectively from 5% and 3.3% in the second quarter. September's price increases were driven largely by a surge in energy costs that economists fear could be spreading to other parts of the economy. Gasoline and other energy goods saw a 9.2% rise for the month while energy goods and services broadly jumped 5.4%. At the same time, services prices excluding energy and housing rose 0.4%, and housing costs increased 0.3%.

items.title: Fed keeps interest rates steady despite rising inflation
items.excerpt: Oct. 28, 2026, 2:01 PM EDT / Updated Oct. 28, 2026, 2:44 PM EDT By Steve Kopack, Maya Huter and Brian Cheung The Federal Reserve voted Wednesday to keep interest rates unchanged, its final monetary policy decision before the midterm elections. The decision to hold rates steady came despite inflation that jumped from a 3.4% annual rate in August to 3.7% in September. ... A major driver of that inflation is the soaring cost of gas, diesel and crude oil. These higher prices have hit consumers hard, and many economists say the spillover effect of rising gas prices has started to show up across the broader economy. In its post-decision statement, the Fed acknowledged the problem that inflation is causing but said it needs more data before moving forward with a rate hike. “Inflation remains elevated. The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 percent goal,” it said. The Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, the personal consumption expenditures price index, will not be released until Thursday; it is expected to touch 3.7%. ... “As we widen the frame to survey the broad economic and financial picture, real activity is clearly pointing in the right direction,” Warsh said in a post-meeting news conference. “That’s good news, but inflation is too high.” “Energy and related prices have moved higher again in recent weeks, and our job is to ensure that relative price changes in some sectors do not broaden out across the economy,” he added. Wednesday’s vote was not unanimous, unlike September’s 12-0 vote to hike rates, the first time since 2023 that the central bank had raised its benchmark rate. Two officials, governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, dissented in favor of a rate hike.

items.excerpt: ## El-Sayed campaign asks Stevens not to attend final campaign events CBS News has confirmed that Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed's campaign has asked his former primary rival, Rep. Haley Stevens, to stay away from all remaining campaign events in the final days before Tuesday's election, according to two sources familiar with the matter. This development, which was first reported by Politico, follows a public dispute between the two Michigan Democrats, who had been expected to make a rare joint appearance Sunday at a Detroit church alongside SC Rep. Jim Clyburn to help galvanize Black voters to support El-Sayed in his Senate race. On Friday, Stevens called on El-Sayed to condemn an outside group's ad linking US military aid to Israel to rising grocery prices, which she characterized as antisemitic. She also called on El-Sayed to apologize for previous remarks that she said linked US support for Israel to Michigan's affordability challenges and urged him to remove a campaign ad featuring conservative commentator Tucker Carlson. El-Sayed's campaign has said it has no affiliation with the outside ad. In a response Friday night, El-Sayed accused Stevens of attempting to rehash their acrimonious Democratic primary battle, saying she "seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago," rather than focusing on defeating Republican Mike Rogers. This comes just days after Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, publicly announced he would vote for Rogers, despite Stevens reaffirming her support for El-Sayed during a CNN interview.

items.title: Justice Department seeks to isolate Alaska ballots amid criminal probe : NPR
items.excerpt: ANCHORAGE, Alaska — The U.S. Department of Justice pushed Friday for a court order to isolate certain Alaska ballots to investigate potential voter confusion, while federal officials confirmed the existence of a criminal probe over a Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent. The dueling developments came days before Tuesday's ranked choice general election, in a race headlined by two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola. The race is among a handful nationwide expected to determine control of the Senate. Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters in Anchorage that the investigation has been ongoing for several months, but recent revelations from The New York Times that Peltola's campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan have resulted in a "significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska." Separately, the Justice Department — as part of a lawsuit it filed last week — asked a judge to order that state elections officials isolate ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan to investigate potential voter "confusion" with the senator. The owner of a boat dealership in the candidate's hometown of Petersburg who had donated to his campaign told The Associated Press that an FBI agent visited the business and wanted to know whether he had been misled by Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy. He said he had not and that "Everybody knows who the incumbent is." Alaska Assistant U.S. Attorney E. Bryan Wilson, in a filing, said the government "seeks to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary." The Department of Justice also filed with the court a list of proposed questions it seeks to compel the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to answer as part of the civil case seeking to block certification of the Senate race if the incumbent loses. President Donald Trump has said he told the department to file the case. ... Peltola denied Thursday that she knew anything about the effort to put Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot: "I am not interested in tricking voters," she said. Democrats, including the DSCC, have repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick. Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats' behest. ... Attorneys for the state in response questioned how segregation would be possible, writing that voters' ballots are commingled in the ballot box on Election Day and that election workers couldn't segregate ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan without violating ballot secrecy protections. Ballots segregated or not wouldn't reveal any voter's reason for voting for Dan J. Sullivan, they said. They have asked a judge to dismiss the case and said Alaska elections officials already took steps to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot. The senator is listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent, while the challenger is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation.

Democrats lead by 51.4 percent to 43.2 percent. A separate Economist/YouGov survey released on Thursday found that 44 percent of registered voters expect Democrats to control the House of Representatives after the election, compared with 31 percent who expect Republicans to retain control. Expectations were much closer for the Senate, with 39 percent expecting a Democratic majority and 36 percent a Republican one. Kyle Kondik, managing editor of Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia Center for Politics, told Al Jazeera that the Democratic lead in national polling suggests a different picture for the two chambers. “A big Democratic lead in House generic ballot polling suggests that the House is almost certain to flip to Democrats,” Kondik said. “However, that does not mean the Senate is going to flip – it certainly could, but it is much more up in the air.”

items.excerpt: 10/31/2026 ... By Isabela Raygoza Associate Editor, Billboard Español Valentín Elizalde Fonovisa Records ## Valentín Elizalde’s Story and Legacy to Be Revisited in New HBO Max Docuseries HBO Max announced on Wednesday (Oct. 28) a three-part documentary series, *Valentín: La muerte del Gallo de Oro*, revisiting the life and 2006 killing of regional Mexican music and banda superstar Valentín Elizalde. Set to premiere Nov. 12, the series will draw on archival material and new voices to revisit questions surrounding the case and the enduring legacy of “El Gallo de Oro.” The announcement has also raised questions about the family’s involvement: Elizalde’s daughter Valentina said publicly that the family had not known about the series and had not authorized it. The project offers a chance to revisit Elizalde’s place in música mexicana, while his family’s concerns remain an important part of the story. ... ## Ozuna Announces One-Night Concert at Puerto Rico’s Coliseo After wrapping his Una Aventura World Tour, Ozuna announced on Tuesday (Oct. 27) that he will return home for Sempiterno, a one-night concert at Puerto Rico’s Coliseo de Puerto Rico José Miguel Agrelot on Dec. 26. The show will celebrate his catalog of hits while offering fans a preview of his next musical chapter. “I’ve been wanting to come back and perform for my people in Puerto Rico for a long time,” the singer said in a statement. “Performing at the Choliseo always means so much to me, and this is my way of thanking my fans for all the love and support they’ve shown me since day one.” Tickets are now on sale through Ticketera. ... ## Rosalía Honored as WSJ. Magazine’s Music Innovator, Sends Support to Spain Rosalía was named Music Innovator at the 16th annual WSJ. Magazine Innovator Awards in New York on Thursday (Oct. 29), joining honorees across fashion, tech, literature, film, sports and comedy. During her acceptance speech, she also paused to acknowledge the deadly train crash in her native Spain and offer support to those affected. “I would like to send all my love and support to each and every person affected by it,” she said in Spanish. The moment paired recognition of Rosalía’s influence on music and culture with a heartfelt gesture of solidarity toward her home country.
